planting.note: Plant container specimens in spring or fall so roots establish before summer heat or winter cold sets in.

directions: Robustum is a coarser, more vigorous laurustinus selection with larger rounded leaves and a faster growth rate than the species, making it a good choice for a quick evergreen screen or informal hedge. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade and water regularly the first year to establish a deep root system. White flower clusters open from pinkish buds in late winter, followed by metallic blue-black fruit that persists into spring. Prune lightly after flowering to control size, since this cultivar can outgrow tighter garden spaces if left unchecked.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring to give roots a full growing season before the first winter.

directions: Gwenllian is a Welsh-raised laurustinus selection prized for its heavy bud set and flowers that emerge deep pink and fade to white, giving a two-tone effect through the winter bloom season. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil and provide shelter from harsh winter wind in the coldest part of its hardiness range. This cultivar tolerates coastal exposure and light shade better than many other evergreen shrubs, making it useful as a mixed-border backdrop or informal screen. Deadheading is unnecessary, but a light shaping prune after flowering keeps growth dense.
sources: American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

planting.note: Plant in spring so the compact root system fills its space before cold weather arrives.

directions: Eve Price is the most compact widely grown laurustinus cultivar, valued for dense, small dark green leaves and deep carmine-pink buds that open to blush-white flowers from midwinter into spring. Its tight habit suits low hedging, foundation plantings, and containers where full-size laurustinus would be too large. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and water during dry spells the first two years to establish. Because it stays naturally neat, pruning needs are minimal beyond an occasional trim to maintain shape.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Transplant container stock in spring into a sheltered site with reliable moisture.

directions: Japanese viburnum is grown for its exceptionally glossy, thick, leathery leaves and clusters of fragrant white flowers borne in late spring, followed by bright red fruit in fall. It performs best in humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture and appreciates afternoon shade in hotter climates, since the broad leaves can scorch in intense sun. Give it a sheltered site protected from drying winter wind, particularly near the cold edge of its range. It combines well with other broadleaf evergreens in a woodland or shade border and needs little pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood.
sources: American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring or early fall in evenly moist soil.

directions: Watanabe is a compact, heavy-reblooming doublefile viburnum that produces flat lacecap flower clusters in late spring and continues to put out sporadic blooms through summer, more reliably than most doublefile types. Its smaller mature size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings or smaller gardens where a full-size doublefile would be too imposing. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in warmer zones. Prune immediately after the main spring flush if shaping is needed, since flower buds for the following season form on old wood.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out plants in spring or early fall and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist.

directions: Newport is a dwarf, densely branched doublefile viburnum that keeps the horizontal tiered branching of the type on a much smaller frame, making it well suited to compact borders or mass planting where space is limited. White lacecap flower clusters line the branches in late spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, providing supplemental water during dry stretches. Its naturally tight, mounded habit needs little pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward shoot.
sources: American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

planting.note: Plant in spring in consistently moist, well-drained soil and mulch to conserve moisture.

directions: Molly Schroeder arose as a sport of a reblooming doublefile viburnum and is notable for lacecap flower clusters that open white and age to soft pink, with intermittent rebloom through summer on a full-sized tiered shrub. Site it in moist, fertile, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in warmer areas, since both flower color and foliage hold up best out of intense midday heat. Give it room to develop its characteristic horizontal branching, since crowding disguises the tiered form that makes doublefile viburnums distinctive. Minimal pruning is needed; remove only dead or crossing branches after the main spring bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil, ideally near another linden viburnum for cross-pollination and heavier fruit set.

directions: Michael Dodge is a linden viburnum selection prized for abundant clear golden-yellow fruit that ripens in fall and persists well into winter, a striking contrast to the typical red-berried species. Flat white flower clusters appear in late spring, and fruit set is heaviest when a different linden viburnum seedling or cultivar is planted nearby as a pollinizer. Grow in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; established plants tolerate short dry spells but color and fruit yield are best with even moisture. Little pruning is required beyond removing old or crowded stems in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall, spacing generously for its eventual use as a dense screen.

directions: Willowwood is a US National Arboretum introduction combining the leathery, textured leaves of leatherleaf viburnum with a looser, more graceful branching habit, holding its dark green foliage semi-evergreen well into winter in milder zones. Flat creamy-white flower clusters appear in late spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black. It is notably drought tolerant once established and adapts to a wide range of soils, making it a low-maintenance choice for a large informal hedge or screen. Prune only to remove damaged wood or to control size, since flower buds form on the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil, giving it full room to develop into a dense screen.

directions: Alleghany is a hardier, more compact US National Arboretum selection than its sibling Willowwood, with glossy dark green leaves that resist Japanese beetle feeding better than many other viburnums. Creamy white flower clusters open in late spring and are followed by heavy sets of red fruit that darken to black as they ripen, attracting birds through fall. It thrives in full sun in average, well-drained soil and tolerates heat, drought, and a wide pH range once established. Use it as a dense, low-care privacy hedge or screen, pruning only lightly to shape after flowering.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil, choosing a site sheltered from harsh winter wind at the colder end of its range.

directions: Eskimo is a compact US National Arboretum hybrid bred for dense, rounded form and abundant snowball-like clusters of pure white flowers in mid-spring, though unlike its fragrant Korean spice viburnum parentage it produces little to no scent. Its semi-evergreen foliage holds late into winter in milder climates, giving structure to the border year-round. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, watering during establishment and dry spells. Its naturally tidy, dwarf habit fits foundation plantings and smaller gardens where full-size viburnums would overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; this dense, spreading hybrid works well as a low informal hedge.

directions: Conoy is a low, wide-spreading US National Arboretum hybrid with small glossy dark green leaves that stay evergreen to semi-evergreen through most of its hardiness range, giving it a refined, fine-textured look compared to coarser-leaved viburnums. Clusters of white flowers appear in mid to late spring, followed by red fruit that matures to black and draws songbirds in fall. It shows good resistance to bacterial leaf spot, a problem that affects several related viburnums, and tolerates full sun to partial shade in average, well-drained soil. Its dense, mounded habit needs only occasional shaping to maintain a tidy hedge or foundation planting.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
